title: DOES DEPRESSION MEAN YOU DON’T TRUST GOD ENOUGH? THEN WHY DID SOME OF GOD’S MOST FAITHFUL SERVANTS BEG FOR THEIR LIVES TO END?
paragraphs: DOES DEPRESSION MEAN YOU DON’T TRUST GOD ENOUGH? THEN WHY DID SOME OF GOD’S MOST FAITHFUL SERVANTS BEG FOR THEIR LIVES TO END?

Before you tell a struggling Christian to pray harder, read what happened to Elijah under a tree, David in the darkness, and Jesus in Gethsemane. Because the Bible tells a story about suffering that many churches have forgotten—and it might change how you see the person silently falling apart beside you.
There is a kind of pain that becomes even heavier when the people who are supposed to help you carry it begin questioning your faith.
Imagine sitting in a church pew, surrounded by people singing about the goodness of God.
Everyone is standing.
Hands are raised.
Voices are strong.
And somewhere in the middle of that congregation is a person who barely found the strength to get out of bed that morning.
They sang the same worship songs.
They whispered the same prayers.
They believed in the same Savior.
But when everyone else went home feeling encouraged, they went home to a darkness they could not explain.
And perhaps the cruelest part was not the depression itself.
It was the question someone planted in their heart.
“If you really trusted God, wouldn't you be happy?”
Maybe someone told them they needed more faith.
Maybe they were warned that depression was evidence of spiritual weakness.
Maybe they heard that Christians should always be joyful because Jesus has already won the victory.
And because they loved Jesus, they began wondering whether something was terribly wrong with them.
They started apologizing to God for feelings they could not control.
They prayed longer.
They tried harder.
They smiled wider.
They hid deeper.
Until eventually, they were no longer just fighting depression.
They were fighting the terrifying suspicion that God was disappointed in them for being depressed.
And that is where this conversation must begin.
Because there is a difference between a soul refusing to trust God and a soul desperately trying to hold on to God while suffering.
Depression is not, by itself, evidence that someone lacks faith.
Read that again.
Not because faith is unimportant.
Not because trusting God does not matter.
But because Scripture never gives us permission to measure someone's relationship with God by how emotionally healthy they appear.
And if we are going to speak in the name of Jesus, we had better be careful not to condemn people He has called us to love.
Consider Elijah.
Not a man who merely attended religious gatherings.
Not someone who occasionally prayed when life became difficult.
Elijah was a prophet who stood against idolatry, confronted wickedness, and witnessed the extraordinary power of the living God.
In 1 Kings 18, he stood on Mount Carmel as God answered with fire.
What a moment.
The kind of miracle that makes people imagine faith must become effortless afterward.
Surely, after witnessing something so spectacular, Elijah would never again experience overwhelming fear or despair.
Surely, a man who had seen fire fall from heaven would never struggle to face another morning.
But the very next chapter shatters that assumption.
Jezebel threatened his life.
Elijah became afraid and fled.
He traveled into the wilderness, sat beneath a broom tree, and prayed words that should make every Christian reconsider the way we speak about despair.
“...It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.”
—1 Kings 19:4, King James Version
Stop there.
Let the weight of that moment settle.
This was Elijah.
The prophet who had confronted kings.
The man who had witnessed the fire of God.
And now he was sitting alone beneath a tree, asking God to let him die.
Was Elijah suddenly a worthless servant?
Had every previous act of faith been erased by one season of despair?
Did God look down from heaven and say, “You should be ashamed of yourself”?
No.
Look carefully at what happened next.
Elijah fell asleep.
An angel touched him and told him to arise and eat.
There was bread.
There was water.
There was rest.
And then, after Elijah slept again, the angel returned and provided more nourishment.
“Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee.”
—1 Kings 19:7, KJV
Those words are extraordinary.
The journey was too great for him.
God did not deny Elijah's exhaustion.
He did not pretend the prophet had unlimited strength.
He did not treat a suffering human being as though he were a machine that could run forever on spiritual enthusiasm.
He provided for his physical needs.
And later, God spoke to him, corrected his mistaken belief that he was the only faithful one left, and gave him further direction and companionship through the calling of Elisha.
This passage does not establish a clinical diagnosis of depression for Elijah. Scripture does not use modern psychiatric categories to describe him.
But it unquestionably shows a faithful servant experiencing profound fear, exhaustion, isolation, and a desire to die.
And God's response should humble anyone who believes that spiritual maturity makes a person immune to emotional suffering.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing a suffering person needs is not another accusation about their faith, but the kind of compassionate care God gave Elijah.
Food.
Rest.
Safety.
Presence.
Truth.
And help for the journey ahead.
Now consider something even more uncomfortable.
What if the person sitting beside you in church has been praying faithfully for months, perhaps years, while living with major depressive disorder?
What if their exhaustion is not laziness?
What if their difficulty concentrating is not indifference toward Scripture?
What if their inability to feel pleasure is not proof that they have stopped loving God?
What if their tears are not rebellion?
What if their silence is not spiritual coldness?
What if they are fighting an illness that affects mood, energy, sleep, appetite, thinking, and the ability to function?
Depression is a real health condition, not simply a bad attitude or a decision to stop trusting God.
It can involve biological, psychological, social, and environmental factors. Sometimes its causes are complicated and difficult to identify.
And while spiritual struggles can accompany depression, the presence of depression alone cannot tell us whether someone trusts God.
We would not ordinarily tell a Christian with pneumonia that their fever proves they have abandoned the Lord.
We would not tell someone with diabetes that needing medical care automatically demonstrates unbelief.
Why, then, should we assume that every disorder affecting the mind must be the consequence of inadequate prayer?
The brain is part of the body.
And human beings are not merely disembodied spirits waiting to escape their physical limitations.
We are embodied creatures.
Created by God.
Affected by weakness.
Living in a world where suffering, illness, and death remain present.
Christian faith does not require us to pretend otherwise.
The apostle Paul understood that weakness and faithfulness can exist in the same life.
In 2 Corinthians 1:8, he described affliction in Asia with astonishing honesty:
“...we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life.”
—2 Corinthians 1:8, KJV
Paul was not necessarily describing clinical depression.
He was describing overwhelming suffering.
But notice what he did not do.
He did not edit his testimony to make himself sound invincible.
He did not hide the fact that his circumstances had pushed him beyond what he could endure in his own strength.
He told the truth.
And that truth has been preserved in Scripture for generations.
Maybe we need to ask ourselves why the Bible is more honest about human suffering than some of our Christian conversations.
Because somewhere along the way, many believers learned to confuse appearing strong with actually trusting God.
We began treating tears as spiritual failure.
We mistook emotional numbness for spiritual emptiness.
We turned “rejoice in the Lord” into a demand that suffering Christians must always look cheerful.
But biblical joy is not the same thing as uninterrupted happiness.
Christian joy is rooted in who God is and what Christ has accomplished, even when our emotions are troubled.
A believer can possess genuine hope in Christ while struggling to experience positive feelings.
And the command to rejoice must be understood within the whole counsel of Scripture, which also commands us to weep with those who weep.
Romans 12:15 does not say, “Correct those who weep until they become cheerful.”
It says:
“Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
There is a ministry of presence that cannot be replaced by religious slogans.
Sometimes love sounds like, “I don't fully understand what you're experiencing, but I'm not leaving you to face it alone.”
Sometimes it sounds like, “Have you been able to eat?”
Sometimes it sounds like, “Would you like me to accompany you to an appointment?”
Sometimes it sounds like, “You don't have to pretend with me.”
And sometimes it sounds like nothing at all.
Just someone sitting beside you.
Not rushing.
Not judging.
Not turning your suffering into an opportunity to demonstrate how many Bible verses they have memorized.
Just staying.
Because love is patient.
And people in deep pain need more than explanations.
They need compassion.
Now open the Psalms.
Listen to David.
Not the polished version of David we sometimes imagine.
Not merely the giant-slayer.
Not simply the king with a harp.
Listen to the man whose prayers included fear, sorrow, guilt, loneliness, and desperate cries for deliverance.
Psalm 42:5 asks:
“Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God...”
The Hebrew phrase behind “cast down” includes the verb שׁוּחַ (shuaḥ), expressing the idea of being bowed down or brought low.
The word translated “disquieted” comes from הָמָה (hamah), which can describe tumult, agitation, or inward unrest.
These are not sterile theological concepts.
They describe the turmoil of a human soul.
And notice something beautiful.
The psalmist does not pretend the turmoil is absent.
He addresses it.
He brings it into conversation with hope.
“Hope thou in God.”
The Hebrew word יָחַל (yachal) carries the sense of waiting or hoping.
This is not the voice of someone who has already escaped every painful emotion.
It is the voice of someone calling his troubled soul to wait for God.
That distinction matters.
Faith is not always the immediate disappearance of sorrow.
Sometimes faith is the trembling decision to keep turning toward God while sorrow remains.
Sometimes it is opening your Bible and reading only one verse because concentration feels impossible.
Sometimes it is whispering the name of Jesus when you cannot form a longer prayer.
Sometimes it is accepting help because you recognize that God often cares for His people through other people.
And sometimes it is saying, “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief,” echoing the desperate father in Mark 9:24.
Jesus did not reject that father for admitting his struggle.
He met him in the middle of it.
But there is an even deeper place we must go.
A place where the ground itself seems sacred beneath our feet.
Gethsemane.
The night before the crucifixion.
Jesus knew what was approaching.
Betrayal.
Arrest.
Humiliation.
Suffering.
The cross.
And Matthew records something that should forever change the way Christians speak about emotional anguish.
“Then saith he unto them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me.”
—Matthew 26:38, KJV
In the Greek text, Jesus says:
περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου
Perilypos estin hē psychē mou heōs thanatou.
A faithful rendering is:
“My soul is deeply sorrowful, even to the point of death.”
The Greek adjective περίλυπος (perilypos) communicates profound sorrow or distress.
It is a powerful expression.
And who spoke it?
Jesus Christ.
The sinless Son of God.
The One who perfectly trusted His Father.
The One whose obedience never failed.
We must be precise here.
Gethsemane does not mean Jesus had clinical depression.
Scripture does not diagnose Him with a depressive disorder, and it would be irresponsible to force a modern medical diagnosis onto this sacred moment.
But Gethsemane establishes something beyond dispute.
Profound emotional anguish is not inherently sinful, because the sinless Savior Himself experienced profound emotional anguish.
Jesus was sorrowful.
Jesus was troubled.
Jesus asked His disciples to remain near Him.
Jesus prayed.
And He submitted Himself to the Father's will.
“...nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
—Matthew 26:39, KJV
His sorrow did not cancel His obedience.
His distress did not make His trust imperfect.
His anguish was not evidence of moral failure.
So when a Christian experiences severe emotional suffering, we must not automatically label that suffering as unbelief.
We cannot use Gethsemane to explain every cause of depression.
But we can use it to dismantle the cruel idea that experiencing intense sorrow necessarily means someone has failed God.
And there is something else here.
Jesus asked His disciples to watch with Him.
The Savior who could have summoned heavenly armies chose to bring His closest companions into that hour.
How much more should we recognize the importance of human companionship when ordinary people are overwhelmed?
No, this does not mean every struggle can be solved by friendship.
Clinical depression may require professional assessment, psychotherapy, medication, or a combination of treatments.
But it does mean that seeking support is not something Christians should automatically be ashamed of.
Prayer and medical care are not enemies.
Scripture and sound treatment are not competing saviors.
A physician is not a replacement for Christ.
A counselor is not the Holy Spirit.
Medication is not redemption.
But neither does the Bible teach that receiving appropriate medical treatment is a betrayal of God.
Luke, a companion of Paul, is identified as “the beloved physician” in Colossians 4:14.
And while that verse is not a complete theology of mental healthcare, it certainly does not portray the medical vocation as inherently unspiritual.
God can work through prayer.
Through the wisdom of Scripture.
Through pastors who understand their responsibilities and limitations.
Through loving families.
Through trained mental health professionals.
Through appropriate treatment.
Through ordinary acts of care that keep a suffering person connected to life.
These things need not compete.
They can serve different, complementary purposes.
And please hear this.
If you have been diagnosed with depression, taking prescribed medication does not make you a second-class Christian.
Seeing a therapist does not mean Jesus has become insufficient.
Receiving treatment does not mean you have chosen science over God.
It means you are receiving care for a real condition.
Treatment decisions should be made with qualified healthcare professionals, and medication should not be started, stopped, or changed solely because of a religious message.
Your spiritual life deserves attention.
So does your health.
Both matter.
But perhaps someone reading this has an even more painful question.
“What if I have prayed for years and I still feel depressed?”
What if you have fasted?
What if people have prayed over you?
What if you have confessed every sin you can remember?
What if you have memorized promises and listened to worship music and attended church faithfully?
And still, there are mornings when the weight returns.
Does that mean God has refused to hear you?
No.
Persistent depression does not prove that God has abandoned you.
And unanswered requests for immediate relief do not prove that your prayers are worthless.
But we must also resist the temptation to promise what Scripture has not promised.
The Bible does not guarantee that every believer will experience complete relief from every illness in this present life.
Paul prayed repeatedly about his thorn in the flesh.
God's answer was not the immediate removal Paul requested.
Instead, Paul heard:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
—2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
We are not told exactly what Paul's thorn was, so we should not identify it as depression.
Yet the passage teaches something essential.
God's grace is not limited to moments when suffering disappears.
Christ can sustain His people in weakness.
That does not mean we should romanticize illness.
It does not mean refusing treatment.
It does not mean telling people to accept avoidable suffering.
It means that the presence of weakness does not place someone beyond the reach of God's grace.
And if you are struggling right now, I want you to notice the difference between two statements.
“God loves me only when I am strong.”
And:
“God loves me in Christ, even when I am weak.”
Only one of those reflects the heart of the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that strong people can earn God's acceptance by maintaining flawless emotional stability.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by the perfection of our emotional lives.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
Depression is not a substitute for repentance, and having a mental illness does not mean a person is incapable of sin.
All of us still need the forgiveness and transforming grace of Christ.
But neither should we turn an illness into an accusation of sin without biblical grounds.
Jesus addressed this kind of careless assumption in John 9.
When His disciples encountered a man born blind, they asked whose sin had caused his condition.
Jesus rejected their proposed explanation.

The circumstances of that passage are different from clinical depression, but the warning remains important: we must not presume to know that another person's suffering is the direct punishment for a particular sin.
How many wounded believers have we burdened because we assumed we knew the spiritual explanation for their pain?
How many have stopped talking because every confession of struggle was answered with correction?
How many have smiled in church while secretly fearing that their suffering made them unacceptable to God?
How many have quietly disappeared because they felt safer being alone than being misunderstood by Christians?
We need to confront this.
Not to attack the church.
But because we love the church.
Because the body of Christ should not become a place where wounded people feel compelled to hide their wounds.
Galatians 6:2 says:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”
Not investigate every burden until we find someone to blame.
Not demand that suffering people recover quickly enough to make us comfortable.
Bear them.
Walk alongside people.
Pray with them.
Encourage them to seek appropriate help.
Speak truth without cruelty.
Offer hope without making promises God has not made.
And remember that spiritual care and clinical treatment address overlapping but distinct needs.
If someone says they are thinking about ending their life, take those words seriously.
Do not dismiss them as attention-seeking.
Do not tell them suicide-related thoughts are merely proof of weak faith.
Stay with them when it is safe to do so, help them reach immediate professional or emergency support, and involve trusted people who can help protect them.
If there is immediate danger, contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
A person in crisis needs urgent compassionate care, not a theological argument.
And perhaps that is one of the clearest ways the church can demonstrate the love of Christ.
By protecting life.
By refusing to abandon the vulnerable.
By remembering that people are not projects.
They are human beings made in God's image.
Now, let me speak to the person who has been reading this while silently holding back tears.
You may have spent months believing that your inability to feel happy meant your faith was defective.
You may have avoided prayer because you felt ashamed.
You may have stopped telling people the truth because their answers made you feel worse.
You may have watched other Christians celebrate victories while you struggled to complete the simplest tasks.
And somewhere inside, you may have begun to wonder whether Jesus had grown tired of you.
Please do not confuse your difficulty feeling God's presence with proof of His absence.
Our feelings are real.
They matter.
They deserve compassionate attention.
But they are not infallible measurements of God's character.
The cross remains the cross even on a morning when you feel emotionally numb.
The resurrection remains true even on a night when you cannot sleep.
The Gospel does not become false because your mind is struggling.
And the invitation of Jesus is not reserved for people who can arrive smiling.
Listen to His words in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word translated “heavy laden” is πεφορτισμένοι (pephortismenoi), a form of φορτίζω (phortizō), meaning to load or burden.
Jesus was speaking within a context of discipleship and the rest found in coming under His gracious instruction, not offering a clinical treatment plan for depression.
Yet His invitation reveals His character.
He calls the burdened to Himself.
He does not tell them to become unburdened before they are welcome.
He does not demand that they manufacture emotional strength as the price of approaching Him.
He invites them to come.
And when we come to Christ, we come not merely to a sympathetic teacher.
We come to the crucified and risen Lord.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who conquered death.
The One who makes reconciliation with God possible.
The One whose grace is greater than our guilt.
This is where our theme becomes more than a phrase.
The scandal is not that a Christian can experience depression.
The scandal is that we have sometimes made suffering believers feel ashamed to admit they need help.
The scandal is that people who should have been met with compassion have sometimes been met with suspicion.
The scandal is that we have occasionally preached grace to sinners while demanding emotional perfection from the wounded.
But grace tells another story.
Grace does not pretend our lives are painless.
Grace does not deny our need for repentance.
Grace does not promise that every difficult chapter will end the way we want.
Grace brings us to Jesus Christ, where forgiveness is offered to sinners, mercy is extended to the needy, and transformation begins through the work of God.
The Gospel does not say that every wound will vanish before heaven.
It says that because Jesus died and rose again, suffering and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Revelation 21:4 points us toward the promised future when God will wipe away every tear and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise is not an excuse to neglect suffering people today.
It is a reason to love them faithfully while we wait.
And perhaps the person who most needs to understand this article is not the person experiencing depression.
Perhaps it is the husband who keeps telling his wife to be more positive.
The parent who thinks their struggling child simply needs discipline.
The pastor who has never been trained to recognize a mental health crisis.
The friend who keeps quoting verses but has never asked, “How can I help you get the support you need?”
Or the believer who has secretly judged people whose suffering they have never personally experienced.
We can repent of those failures.
We can learn.
We can listen.
We can become more faithful in how we care for one another.
And if you have been wounded by Christians who misunderstood your depression, I will not pretend their words did not hurt.
Some wounds are made deeper because they were inflicted by people we trusted.
But please do not mistake every failure of Christ's followers for the heart of Christ Himself.
Look at Jesus.
Look at how He approached the weary.
Look at how He treated the broken.
Look at how He wept at Lazarus's tomb.
Look at how He welcomed people others pushed aside.
Look at His compassion.
And look at His cross.
There you will see the seriousness of sin, the depth of divine mercy, and the astonishing love of the Savior who gave Himself for us.
He does not call us to deny reality.
He calls us to follow Him in truth.
So if you are depressed, keep seeking appropriate care.
If you need professional help, reach for it.
If your symptoms are persistent, worsening, or interfering with daily life, speak with a qualified healthcare professional.
If you have someone trustworthy who can support you, let them know what you are facing.
Keep bringing your life before God, even if your prayers are short and your emotions are difficult to understand.
You do not have to choose between honest suffering and genuine faith.
And if you are supporting someone with depression, remember this:
Your task is not to become their savior.
Jesus already occupies that place.
Your task is to love your neighbor faithfully.
Listen without immediately correcting.
Encourage without pressuring.
Pray without using prayer as a reason to withhold practical assistance.
And when the situation calls for professional help, support them in getting it.
Because the church does not glorify Christ by pretending people are never ill.
We glorify Him by telling the truth and loving people in ways that reflect His character.
Maybe this article has exposed something painful.
Perhaps you have been harsh toward someone whose suffering you did not understand.
Perhaps you have been harsh toward yourself.
Perhaps you are the one who keeps saying, “I'm fine,” because you are afraid of what people will think if they learn the truth.
You do not need to turn the comment section into a place where you reveal more than you are comfortable sharing.
Not as a claim that your recovery must happen immediately.
Not as a declaration that medical treatment is unnecessary.
But as an expression of hope in the Lord who continues His work in His people.
Or comment, “Pray for me,” if you would welcome prayer and encouragement from this community.
“Lord, teach me to love the hurting.”
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only person struggling.
Someone may finally feel safe enough to seek help.
Someone may reconsider the harsh judgment they have been carrying against themselves.
And that is why this message deserves to travel beyond the people who already agree with it.
Not simply to increase numbers.
But because there may be someone among your friends or relatives who has never told you how much they are hurting.
Someone who still attends church.
Still smiles in photographs.
Still says “God is good.”
And still goes home wondering why they cannot feel better.
Or privately send this to a loved one who needs encouragement, especially if publicly tagging them might expose something personal.
Because our mission is not to build an audience around human personalities.
It is to point people toward Jesus Christ.
Toward the truth of His Word.
Toward the grace that forgives.
Toward the repentance that turns us from sin.
Toward the hope that remains when life becomes difficult.
And toward the transforming power of the Gospel.

Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical teaching, discipleship resources, and Christ-centered encouragement available to more people, including those who may never walk into a church but are willing to read a message that reaches them through their phones.
We want these resources to keep reaching people who are hungry for biblical truth, spiritual nourishment, and meaningful discipleship.
And that ongoing work requires time, effort, resources, and faithful stewardship.
It helps sustain the work of preparing and sharing biblical teaching, developing discipleship materials, and making resources accessible to people who need them.
For those who see their giving as an act of worship, supporting Gospel ministry can be one expression of generosity and stewardship.
But we also want to honor an important biblical distinction.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from pressure or compulsion, but from a willing heart.
And the grace of Jesus Christ cannot be bought.
These products are simply another way to support and share the ministry's message. They are not a measure of anyone's faith.
You can pray for this ministry.
You can make use of the free discipleship resources.
Your worth before God is not measured by what you can financially contribute.
What matters most is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully and people are directed toward Him.
No product can reconcile a sinner to God.
No ministry can replace the Savior.
Only Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again.
Only through Him do we receive the forgiveness, reconciliation, and living hope promised in the Gospel.
A prayer.
Lord Jesus,
You know the people reading these words.
You know the ones who are exhausted.
The ones who have been misunderstood.
The ones who have prayed for relief and are still waiting.
The ones who are afraid to tell anyone how badly they are struggling.
You know the people who feel ashamed of their depression.
And You know those who have unknowingly wounded others with careless words.
Teach us to speak the truth in love.
Give us wisdom to recognize when someone needs medical care, professional support, or urgent protection.
Help us become people who listen before we judge.
Lead those who are suffering toward appropriate treatment, trustworthy companionship, and the comfort of Your Word.
Forgive us for the times we have confused religious appearance with genuine faith.
Forgive us for the times we have added unnecessary burdens to already wounded hearts.
Remind us that salvation rests on Your grace, not on our ability to appear strong.
Help us repent where we have sinned.
Help us receive mercy where we have fallen.
And teach us to carry one another's burdens with humility.
For those walking through depression, grant courage for the next step, wisdom in seeking care, and hope rooted in Your faithfulness.
And when the night feels unbearably long, surround them with people who will help them remain safe and supported.
May Your church become a place where truth is spoken, suffering is acknowledged, and people are loved with the compassion You have shown us.
In Your holy name,
Amen.
Now, before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
Does depression mean someone isn't trusting God enough?
No.
Not by itself.
Depression is not a spiritual examination in which every symptom counts against your faith.
It is not proof that Jesus has rejected you.
It is not evidence that the cross has lost its power.
And it is not a reason for the church to turn away from you.
Trusting God matters deeply.
But trusting God does not mean pretending that illness, grief, trauma, or emotional suffering cannot affect us.
It means turning toward the Lord in the reality of our lives, receiving His Word, and making use of the wise and appropriate help available to us.
It means remembering that Christ is our Savior, even when our feelings are difficult to understand.
It means holding fast to the hope of the resurrection while caring responsibly for the life God has entrusted to us today.
And if you are the person who has been hiding behind a smile because you were terrified that someone would question your faith, please remember this:
You do not need to prove your love for Jesus by suffering in silence.
You can tell the truth.
You can ask for help.
You can receive treatment.
You can rest.
You can cry.
You can pray through tears.
And you can keep following Christ, one difficult day at a time.
The darkness you are walking through is not proof that the Light of the world has stopped loving you.
